entries.english:
[Fragmentary heading: Margrave Friedrich of Brandenburg, Bishop Johann of Würzburg, and Counts Johann, Albrecht, and Georg; 19 May 1437.]

By the grace of God, Friedrich, Margrave of Brandenburg, Erzkämmerer des Heiligen Römischen Reiches and Burggraf zu Nürnberg, makes known openly by this letter to all who see or hear it that, concerning the discord, ill will, and matters that had arisen between the reverend lord, our dear uncle Johann, Bischof zu Würzburg, Eytel Hiltmar in place of the dean, and the lords of the cathedral church of Würzburg and their people on one side, and our dear uncles Johann, Albrecht, and Georg, Grafen zu Wertheim, and their people on the other, they had given us their sealed letters of submission so that we might settle everything amicably and in friendship. Each party had given us its sealed letters concerning the award and settlement made at that time. Since the matters covered by our award between our lord of Würzburg and the aforementioned men of Wertheim have become deeply entangled in legal proceedings, and verdicts and oaths have been pronounced concerning them, there is a danger that further legal proceedings may cause the matters to escalate and bring both sides into still greater ill will and discord. As they have turned to us from both sides, we do not wish to see this. To prevent such discord, with the consent, knowledge, and approval of both parties, we have sought a friendly settlement between them and have fully set aside the legal proceedings they had begun against one another. Since both sides have brought this discord and these matters before us, we now arrange and decide them for the future in friendship and good will, and both parties shall faithfully observe, perform, and carry out our decision, as they have promised us. We therefore decide, order, and declare as follows.

First, all discord, ill will, and dispute between our aforementioned lord of Würzburg, his chapter and their people, and our aforementioned uncles Johann, Albrecht, and Georg, Grafen zu Wertheim, and their people, shall now be wholly ended and settled in an amicable and reconciled manner, except for Peter Wittstat and Schadenfros, who were involved in the affair said to have occurred at Uffenheim. Henceforth neither side shall reproach, aggravate, or avenge anything against the other out of malice or resentment. Rather, our lord of Würzburg shall be a gracious and favorable lord to our aforementioned uncles of Wertheim, protecting, defending, and supporting them lawfully and faithfully as his other counts and vassals; they, in turn, shall be his faithful counts and vassals and serve him and his church of Würzburg faithfully and diligently, without deceit. Under this amicable award, all submissions, claims, demands, and oaths made before us between the two parties up to this day shall be wholly void; neither party may henceforth revive or pursue them in any way, except for what we stipulate and address in this friendly award.

We also decide and declare concerning the 3,000 gulden which we had previously ruled that our lord of Würzburg should pay Count Johann of Wertheim for outlay and expenses at our Frauenberg: the noble Conrad, Herr zu Weinsberg; Ernst, Herr von Hohenlohe; and the honorable and steadfast Weiprecht von Helmstat, Ritter and Hofmeister of our lord of Mainz; and Conrad von Rosenberg zu Partenstein became jointly liable for the debt and gave their letters and seals for it. The aforesaid Count Johann of Wertheim, for himself and all his heirs, shall release our lord of Würzburg, his church, and the aforementioned joint debtors from liability for those 3,000 gulden and the interest accrued on them, and shall provide and send them a proper sealed receipt bearing his attached seal within the next eight days, without delay or deceit.

We further decide concerning the annual life annuity of 200 gulden which our lord of Würzburg, by our award, promised and assigned to Graf Albrecht of Wertheim at Iphofen: Graf Albrecht shall release our lord of Würzburg, his church, and the town of Iphofen from that annual life annuity of 200 gulden, and shall send and deliver to them within the next eight days, without delay, the relevant letters and a proper receipt bearing his attached seal. The 100 gulden of the life annuity falling due at Iphofen this Pentecost are excepted; our lord shall pay those 100 gulden to Graf Albrecht of Wertheim without hindrance or deceit.

As we previously stated in our award concerning debts, our lord of Würzburg was to relieve Graf Albrecht of all debts which our lord had handed over to him to settle during the period when he was administrator, in whatever amount they then stood or had since changed, and was also to assume any resulting losses and free Graf Albrecht from them. We now decide concerning the debts that Graf Albrecht incurred with our lord of Würzburg during the time from their coming together until their falling out: our lord of Würzburg shall once again assume all the above-mentioned debts for which he has not yet made himself liable, and shall be and remain liable to the creditors for payment; Graf Albrecht shall not be liable. Our lord shall also release Graf Albrecht’s seal from liability for those debts between now and the coming feast of Saint James, without delay or deceit. Concerning the debts which we retained for ourselves, we decide that our lord of Würzburg shall assume the following debts, be liable to the creditors for their payment, and free Graf Albrecht of Wertheim from liability. He shall also release Graf Albrecht’s seal from liability for these debts between now and the coming feast of Saint James, without delay or deceit.

The debts are as follows: 300 gulden for oxen owed to a man of Landshut; 65 gulden to Amelung of Erfurt for stockfish; 93 gulden to Schilher the butcher of Würzburg for meat; 57 gulden to Hans Feren of Schweinfurt for the prisoners’ expenses; 90 gulden to six knights at the regional court, namely Erelbeck, Hiltprant, and others; 44 gulden to Henckelein, a merchant of Würzburg, for spices and other goods taken from him; 2,000 gulden to the men of Hohenriette, Bopfinger, and Liebenstein, whom Graf Albrecht captured; 110 gulden to Zayssolff of Alatzheim for his earned wages and damages; 150 gulden to Peter Haberkorn for his losses and also for wine; 17 gulden to Lord Hans Winter zu Lar for wood, and 25 gulden to the same Winter for oats; 103½ gulden to Hans von Leynach for oats; 80 gulden to the man of Weinsberg for kitchen provisions on behalf of the men of Öllingen; 14 gulden to Abraham the Jew; 950 gulden to Hiltprant von Robiss for his losses in the defeat and to Hans Harandt. Also, because the canons of Würzburg had property taken from them at Ochsenfurt and Würzburg, our aforementioned uncles Johann, Albrecht, and Georg, Grafen zu Wertheim, and their people are not liable for it and are innocent of it; therefore they shall not be required to answer for or make claims concerning any of that seized property, in court or out of court, spiritual or temporal, in any way whatsoever, without deceit.

Concerning the guns—the Triererin and the others—we decide and declare that our aforementioned uncles of Wertheim shall faithfully and without delay deliver all those guns to our lord by the coming feast of Saint Vitus, including the guns which were delivered to Master Michel of Wertheim of the Teutonic Order. For any guns that remained with our lord and were not delivered, and for any of the aforesaid guns that were lost, the Grafen von Wertheim shall pay our lord of Würzburg such compensation as we determine, without deceit. As for the matter of Pütt—[the text is damaged here]—we have nothing further to decide. As we previously ruled concerning Graf Albrecht and the New Minster of Würzburg, regarding the fruits, our award shall remain in force, and on that point the prior ruling remains unchanged.

For true confirmation of all this, we have caused our attached seal to be placed on this amicable decision for the aforementioned parties. And we, Johann, by the grace of God Bishop of Würzburg; Eytel Hiltmar the Elder, acting in the dean’s place; the lords of the cathedral chapter; and we, Johann, Albrecht, and Georg, the aforementioned Grafen von Wertheim, acknowledge in this letter that these agreements, arrangements, provisions, and decisions have been made with our good will, knowledge, and approval, at the request of the aforesaid lords, our friends, and our gracious lord. We promise in good faith faithfully to keep, perform, and carry out all and each of the matters addressed in the above award, and not to act against it, in or out of court, spiritual or temporal, in any way whatsoever, without deceit. In witness of all this, we have caused our seals to be attached to this letter alongside the seal of the aforementioned lord, friend, and gracious lord, the Margrave. Done and given at Kitzingen on the holy day of Pentecost, in the year of our Lord 1437.

[The source then appends another document, with a damaged opening:] Reversal of the town of Wertheim concerning its freedom from paying hand money and toll, granted to it by Count Johann of Wertheim, revocable at will, dated 29 July 1437. We, the following named, namely the Schultheiss, mayors, aldermen, and burghers of the town of Wertheim, rich and poor alike, jointly acknowledge and make known to everyone, for ourselves and our successors, by this letter: the noble lord Count Johann, Count of Wertheim, our gracious lord, has granted us particular aid and favor and has set it down in an open letter sealed by his grace, which we possess and which reads word for word as written below. It begins thus: “We, Johann, Count of Wertheim, openly acknowledge and make known by this open letter, for ourselves, our heirs, and our county, that since our dear and faithful Schultheiss, mayors, aldermen, and burghers, rich and poor alike, in our town of Wertheim are burdened and overburdened each year by heavy and onerous levies, taxes, rents, dues, and many other obligations, we have granted them, as a counter-support and aid, this favor and freedom, and hereby grant it by force of this letter, as follows: all goods which the aforesaid Schultheiss, mayors, aldermen, and burghers, rich and poor alike, of our town of Wertheim own within our district of Wertheim shall henceforth be exempt from paying us or our heirs any hand money. Furthermore, if outsiders buy wine or other merchandise in our town of Wertheim and carry it away overland, they shall pay us on those goods …” [the supplied transcription ends here].
